title: Through the Stealth Lens: Attention-Aware Defenses Against Poisoning in RAG
claim: A poisoned passage draws outsized attention, and filtering attention-score outliers before generation restores the correct answer.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, attention bars beside passages, funnel filter in middle
description: A left-to-right pipeline on a pale blue background, built around a Sagrada Familia question-answering example. On the left, a user icon sends a query, and a retriever icon returns a stack of passages. Most passages are blue-gray and say five of six towers are complete, with green-highlighted answers. One passage is pink, has a devil icon, and says 3 in red. Beside each passage is a small bar showing its normalized attention score. The poisoned passage has a large red bar at 37%, and the benign passages have blue bars at 4–6%. A bracket leads to an LLM icon that outputs Answer: 3 with a red X. A mini variance histogram and a funnel labeled AV Filter come next. On the right, the poisoned passage is removed and the remaining passages have uniform bars. A second LLM then outputs Answer: 5 with a green check.
caption: AV Filter Overview. The retriever returns passages $z^{(k)}$, one of which is poisoned and disproportionately influences the response, increasing variance in NPAS across passages. AV Filter mitigates this by removing passages with anomalously high attention scores, indicative of poisoning.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to attacks that inject poisoned passages into the retrieved context, even at low corruption rates. We show that existing attacks are not designed to be stealthy, allowing reliable detection and mitigation. We formalize a distinguishability-based security game to quantify stealth for such attacks. If a few poisoned passages control the response, they must bias the inference process more than the benign ones, inherently compromising stealth. This motivates analyzing intermediate signals of LLMs, such as attention weights, to approximate the influence of different passages on the response. Leveraging attention weights, we introduce the $\textbf{Normalized Passage Attention Score}$ (NPAS) and a lightweight $\textbf{Attention-Variance Filter}$ (AV Filter) that flags anomalous passages. Our method improves robustness, yielding up to $\sim$ $\textbf{20%}$ higher accuracy than baseline defenses. We also develop adaptive attacks that attempt to conceal such anomalies, achieving up to $\textbf{35%}$ success rate and underscoring the challenges of achieving true stealth in poisoning RAG systems.
